title: The ward office: registration, My Number, insurance & pension
intro:
Your city or ward office ({市役所[しやくしょ]} or {区役所[くやくしょ]}) is where you become an official resident. Within 14 days of moving in, go there with your residence card and passport and file a moving-in notification ({転入届[てんにゅうとどけ]}). Staff will print your address on the back of your residence card. You can usually handle several things in the same visit:

- **Resident registration**. Once registered, you can request a certificate of residence ({住民票[じゅうみんひょう]}), which banks, employers and others often ask for.
- **My Number**. Every resident is assigned a 12-digit personal number used for tax, social security and other administration. A notification is mailed to your registered address, and you can apply for a My Number card, a photo ID that also works as a health insurance card and lets you get some certificates at convenience stores.
- **Health insurance**. If your employer enrolls you in its health insurance ({社会保険[しゃかいほけん]}), you use that. Otherwise you join National Health Insurance ({国民健康保険[こくみんけんこうほけん]}) at the office.
- **Pension**. Residents aged 20 to 59 are generally part of the public pension system: through the employee pension if you work for a company, or the national pension ({国民年金[こくみんねんきん]}) otherwise.

Rules, fees and required documents differ by municipality and change over time, so check your city's website (many have English pages) or ask at the counter. If you move again, file a moving-out notification ({転出届[てんしゅつとどけ]}) at your old office first, and do the same when you leave Japan.

phrases.jp: どの窓口[まどぐち]に行[い]けばいいですか。

phrases.jp: 番号札[ばんごうふだ]を取[と]って、お待[ま]ちください。

phrases.jp: この用紙[ようし]の書[か]き方[かた]を教[おし]えていただけますか。

phrases.jp: 会社[かいしゃ]の健康[けんこう]保険[ほけん]に入[はい]る予定[よてい]です。
phrases.en: I'm going to be on my company's health insurance.

phrases.en: I'd like to apply for a My Number card.

phrases.jp: 住民票[じゅうみんひょう]を一通[いっつう]お願[ねが]いします。
phrases.en: One copy of my certificate of residence, please.

phrases.en: I'm the head of the household.
phrases.note: Forms ask for the {世帯主[せたいぬし]}. If you live alone, it is you.

phrases.jp: 本人[ほんにん]確認[かくにん]書類[しょるい]は何[なに]が必要[ひつよう]ですか。
phrases.en: What ID documents do I need?

phrases.jp: 印鑑[いんかん]は必要[ひつよう]ですか。
phrases.en: Do I need a personal seal (hanko)?

phrases.jp: 年金[ねんきん]の手続[てつづ]きもここでできますか。
phrases.en: Can I do the pension procedure here too?

phrases.jp: 英語[えいご]の案内[あんない]はありますか。
phrases.en: Do you have information in English?

phrases.jp: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]すので、転出届[てんしゅつとどけ]を出[だ]したいです。
phrases.en: I'm moving, so I'd like to file a moving-out notification.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.jp: 次[つぎ]の方[かた]、どうぞ。本日[ほんじつ]はどのようなご用件[ようけん]でしょうか。
dialogue.en: Next, please. How can I help you today?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 先週[せんしゅう]、日本[にほん]に来[き]ました。住所[じゅうしょ]の登録[とうろく]をしたいんですが。
dialogue.en: I arrived in Japan last week. I'd like to register my address.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.jp: 転入[てんにゅう]の届[とど]け出[で]ですね。在留[ざいりゅう]カードとパスポートはお持[も]ちですか。
dialogue.en: A moving-in notification, then. Do you have your residence card and passport?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.jp: ありがとうございます。こちらの届出書[とどけでしょ]に、ご住所[じゅうしょ]とお名前[なまえ]をご記入[きにゅう]ください。
dialogue.en: Thank you. Please fill in your address and name on this form.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 健康[けんこう]保険[ほけん]はどうすればいいですか。
dialogue.en: What should I do about health insurance?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.jp: お勤[つと]め先[さき]で健康[けんこう]保険[ほけん]に加入[かにゅう]されますか。
dialogue.en: Will you be enrolled in health insurance through your employer?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: いいえ、まだ仕事[しごと]が決[き]まっていません。
dialogue.en: No, I haven't found a job yet.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.jp: では、国民健康保険[こくみんけんこうほけん]の手続[てつづ]きが必要[ひつよう]です。こちらが終[お]わりましたら、3番[さんばん]の窓口[まどぐち]へお越[こ]しください。
dialogue.en: Then you'll need to enroll in National Health Insurance. When we're done here, please go to counter 3.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: わかりました。ありがとうございます。

tips: Go early on a weekday and avoid the weeks around late March and early April, when huge numbers of people move.
Watch your mail after registering. Your My Number notification and other official letters arrive by post; do not throw away envelopes from the city.

Keep your pension records. If you leave Japan permanently, you may be able to claim a lump-sum withdrawal payment of part of your contributions; check the Japan Pension Service for current conditions.
If you cannot afford National Health Insurance or pension payments, ask about reductions or exemptions rather than just not paying. Unpaid amounts can cause problems later, including at visa renewal.
Bring a Japanese-speaking friend or use a translation app for your first visit. Many offices also have multilingual consultation services.
